title: Graphs
tagline: The most general structure in CS — vertices, edges, and the two traversals that underpin half of all algorithms.

sections.content:
Most data structures enforce a strict shape on the relationships between items. Arrays demand a linear sequence. Trees demand a hierarchical parent-child structure with exactly one root and no cycles. Linked lists demand a single chain. **Graphs impose almost none of these constraints.** A graph is simply a set of items — called **vertices** (or nodes) — and a set of connections between them — called **edges**. Any pair of vertices can be connected in any direction, and a single vertex can have zero connections or thousands.

This generality is why graphs appear everywhere. Your LinkedIn connections form a graph. The roads between cities form a graph. The hyperlinks between web pages form a graph — Google's original PageRank algorithm ranked pages by analyzing this link graph. Package dependencies in npm or pip form a directed graph. Neural networks are computational graphs. The electrical circuits on your CPU are planar graphs. Even a tree is just a special case of a graph: one that is connected, undirected, and has no cycles.

The two fundamental algorithms for exploring graphs — **Breadth-First Search (BFS)** and **Depth-First Search (DFS)** — are among the most important algorithms in all of computer science. Together they are the basis for shortest path finding, connected component analysis, cycle detection, topological ordering, network flow, and dozens of other problems. Understanding graphs is not optional for a software engineer who wants to reason about complex systems.

In this chapter we will build up graphs from first principles: formal definitions, the two standard representations and when to choose each, a complete treatment of BFS and DFS with worked examples, cycle detection, topological sort, and a survey of the most important real-world graph problems. We will end with weighted graphs and a conceptual introduction to Dijkstra's algorithm. By the end, you will be able to look at any problem and recognize whether it is a graph problem — often the hardest step.

sections.title: Cities, Roads, and Flight Routes
sections.content:
Imagine a country with cities and roads. **Cities are vertices. Roads are edges.** An **undirected** graph models two-lane highways: if you can drive from Paris to Lyon, you can also drive from Lyon to Paris — the relationship is symmetric. A **directed** graph models one-way streets: an edge from A to B does not automatically mean an edge from B to A.

A **weighted** graph assigns a numeric cost to each road — perhaps distance in kilometres, or average travel time, or toll fees. Finding the cheapest flight route between two airports is exactly the classic weighted-graph shortest-path problem (solved by Dijkstra's algorithm). Checking whether two cities are reachable from each other at all is a reachability query answered by BFS or DFS.

Now extend the analogy. Add a rule: some roads are one-way, and there is a cycle of one-way roads that trap you in a loop — that is a **directed cycle**. A city might be isolated with no roads at all — that is an isolated vertex, and the graph is **disconnected**. A city with roads to every other city is a **hub vertex** with high degree. The richness of the map metaphor scales all the way to real algorithms: Google Maps literally runs Dijkstra (or A*) on a weighted directed graph of road segments to compute driving directions.

sections.title: Formal Definitions and Vocabulary
sections.content:
Before we can talk precisely about algorithms we need precise vocabulary.

A **graph** G is defined as a pair (V, E) where V is a set of vertices and E is a set of edges. Each edge is a pair (u, v) of vertices. In an **undirected** graph, the pair is unordered — (u, v) and (v, u) are the same edge. In a **directed** graph (digraph), the pair is ordered — (u, v) means an arrow from u to v, which is a different edge from (v, u).

The **degree** of a vertex is the number of edges incident to it. In a directed graph we distinguish **in-degree** (edges coming in) from **out-degree** (edges going out). A vertex with degree 0 is **isolated**.

A **path** is a sequence of vertices v₁, v₂, …, vₖ where each consecutive pair (vᵢ, vᵢ₊₁) is an edge. The **length** of a path is typically the number of edges (or the sum of edge weights in a weighted graph). A **cycle** is a path that starts and ends at the same vertex with at least one edge.

A graph is **connected** if there is a path between every pair of vertices. A directed graph is **strongly connected** if you can reach every vertex from every other vertex following edge directions. Individual maximally-connected subsets are called **connected components** (undirected) or **strongly connected components** (directed).

A **tree** is a connected undirected graph with no cycles. Equivalently: a connected graph with exactly V−1 edges. A **forest** is a collection of trees (an acyclic undirected graph). A **directed acyclic graph (DAG)** has directed edges and no directed cycles — it models dependency relationships where nothing depends on itself transitively.

A graph is **sparse** if |E| is much smaller than |V|². It is **dense** if |E| is close to |V|². Most real-world graphs (social networks, road maps, the web) are sparse — each node has a small number of connections relative to the total number of nodes.

sections.title: Graph Representations: Adjacency List vs Adjacency Matrix
sections.content:
Every graph algorithm needs a concrete data structure to represent the graph in memory. Two representations dominate practice, each with different trade-offs.

**Adjacency List** maps each vertex to the list of its neighbours. In JavaScript this is typically a `Map` (or plain object) where each key is a vertex and each value is an array of adjacent vertices. For a directed graph, vertex u's list contains only the vertices u has outgoing edges to. For an undirected graph, if (u, v) is an edge, v appears in u's list and u appears in v's list.

Space: **O(V + E)** — one slot per vertex plus one slot per directed edge. This is the correct complexity because the total size of all neighbour lists equals the number of directed edges (2E for undirected since each edge is stored twice, still O(E)). For a sparse graph with millions of vertices and only a few edges per vertex, this is dramatically more compact than the alternative.

Listing all neighbours of vertex u: **O(degree(u))** — just iterate the list. Checking whether edge (u, v) exists: **O(degree(u))** — scan the list for v. Iterating all edges: **O(V + E)**.

**Adjacency Matrix** is a V×V grid of booleans (or weights). `matrix[u][v] = 1` means edge (u, v) exists; `matrix[u][v] = 0` means it does not. For an undirected graph the matrix is symmetric.

Space: **O(V²)** always — even if the graph has only one edge, you allocate space for all V² cells. For a graph with 10,000 vertices, this is 10,000² = 100 million cells. For most real-world graphs this is prohibitive.

Checking whether edge (u, v) exists: **O(1)** — a single array lookup. Listing all neighbours of u: **O(V)** — scan the entire row. Iterating all edges: **O(V²)**.

**Which to choose?** The default answer is: **adjacency list**. The vast majority of real-world graphs are sparse. Use an adjacency matrix only when the graph is dense (E ≈ V²) or when your algorithm needs constant-time edge existence checks so frequently that the O(V) neighbour scan of the list becomes the bottleneck. Floyd-Warshall all-pairs shortest paths is a classic example where the matrix representation makes the algorithm natural to implement.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Both representations encode the same graph. The list is lean for sparse graphs but requires scanning to check a specific edge. The matrix gives O(1) edge checks at the cost of O(V²) memory. In interviews, default to the adjacency list unless the problem says 'dense graph' or requires rapid edge existence checks.

sections.title: Breadth-First Search — Level by Level
sections.content:
**Breadth-First Search (BFS)** is the algorithmic equivalent of spreading ripples from a stone dropped in water. Starting from a source vertex, BFS visits all vertices at distance 1 (direct neighbours), then all at distance 2, then distance 3, and so on — processing the graph in concentric shells.

The key data structure is a **queue** (FIFO). The algorithm:
1. Enqueue the start vertex and mark it visited.
2. Dequeue a vertex u.
3. For each unvisited neighbour v of u: mark v visited, record its distance as dist[u]+1, and enqueue v.
4. Repeat from step 2 until the queue is empty.

**Why BFS guarantees shortest paths in unweighted graphs:** When BFS first reaches a vertex v, it arrives via a path of minimum length. This is because BFS processes all vertices at distance k before any vertex at distance k+1. The first time v is dequeued, no shorter path could exist — if one did, it would have been processed in an earlier wave. This argument breaks down for weighted graphs because a longer edge-count path might have smaller total weight — that is when you need Dijkstra's algorithm.

**Time and space complexity:** Every vertex is enqueued at most once — O(V). Every edge is examined at most once (when processing the source endpoint) — O(E). Total: **O(V + E)**. Space for the visited set and queue is also O(V).

**Practical uses of BFS:** Shortest path in mazes and grid puzzles; finding the minimum number of moves in board games; social network distance ('degrees of separation'); web crawler level-by-level page discovery; network broadcasting (packets flooding a network); bipartite graph checking; finding all vertices in a connected component.

sections.title: Depth-First Search — Dive Deep, Then Backtrack

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The BFS uses a pointer (`head`) instead of `Array.shift()` — shift is O(n), making naive BFS O(V·E). The pointer trick keeps BFS truly O(V+E). DFS entry/exit timestamps are the foundation of topological sort and strongly-connected-component algorithms — a vertex u is an ancestor of v in the DFS tree if and only if enter[u] < enter[v] < exit[v] < exit[u].

sections.title: Cycle Detection — Finding Loops in the Graph
sections.content:
A **cycle** exists when there is a path from some vertex back to itself. Detecting cycles is crucial for many applications: package managers must ensure no circular dependencies; task schedulers must ensure no circular waits (deadlock detection); compilers must verify that import graphs are acyclic.

**In undirected graphs:** During DFS, if we encounter a vertex that is already visited and it is not the direct parent we came from, there is a cycle. The 'not the parent' exception is necessary because in an undirected graph, the edge (u, v) appears in both u's and v's adjacency lists — when DFS at v looks at its neighbours, it sees u (where it just came from). That back-reference is not a cycle; it is just the undirected edge we used to arrive.

**In directed graphs:** The parent-exception trick does not work — a directed graph can have a back edge to a vertex that is not the immediate parent. Instead, we use the **three-colour (WHITE/GRAY/BLACK)** marking scheme:
- WHITE: not yet visited
- GRAY: currently on the DFS call stack (being explored)
- BLACK: fully explored (all descendants processed)

If DFS from vertex u reaches a neighbour v that is GRAY, it means v is an ancestor of u in the current DFS path — an edge from u to its ancestor is precisely a **back edge**, which is exactly a directed cycle. Edges to BLACK vertices are not cycles (the DFS subtree at v is already complete).

**Kahn's BFS-based cycle detection** (for directed graphs): Compute in-degrees for all vertices. Enqueue all vertices with in-degree 0. Repeatedly dequeue a vertex, decrement the in-degree of its neighbours, and enqueue any that reach in-degree 0. At the end, if the output list has fewer vertices than the total, those missing vertices are part of a cycle — they never reached in-degree 0 because their cycle never allowed all incoming edges to be removed first.

sections.title: Topological Sort — Ordering Dependencies
sections.content:
**Topological sort** takes a DAG (directed acyclic graph) and produces a linear ordering of vertices such that for every directed edge (u → v), vertex u appears before v in the output. It is only defined for DAGs — cycles make it impossible, because u must come before v but v must also come before u.

Why does this matter? Build systems (like Make, Gradle, or Webpack) must compile or bundle files in dependency order. If file A imports from file B, B must be compiled first — topological sort finds the safe compilation order. Package managers must install packages in dependency order. Course curriculum planners must schedule prerequisites before the courses that require them.

**DFS-based topological sort:** Run DFS on all vertices. When a vertex finishes (all its descendants are fully explored), push it onto a stack. The final topological order is the stack read top-to-bottom. Why? Finishing a vertex u after all its descendants means u's position in the sort should come before all those descendants — and reversing the finish order gives exactly the topological order.

**Kahn's algorithm (BFS-based):** Compute the in-degree of every vertex. Collect all vertices with in-degree 0 into a queue (these are the 'roots' with no prerequisites). Repeatedly dequeue vertex u, add it to the output, and for each neighbour v reduce in-degree[v] by 1 — if in-degree[v] becomes 0, enqueue v. If the output contains all V vertices, it is a valid topological order. If any vertices are missing, those vertices are in a cycle — topological sort doubles as cycle detection.

Both approaches run in **O(V + E)** time. Kahn's algorithm is often preferred in practice because it is non-recursive (avoiding stack overflow), naturally detects cycles, and is easier to understand.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Kahn's algorithm catches cycles when `result.length < vertices.length` — the vertices stuck in a cycle never reach in-degree 0. The three-colour DFS is more direct: GRAY means 'currently on the recursion stack', and an edge into a GRAY vertex is a back edge. For undirected graphs, simplify to a two-colour visited set with a parent parameter to avoid flagging the edge you arrived on.

sections.title: Connected Components and Graph Connectivity
sections.content:
A **connected component** of an undirected graph is a maximal set of vertices such that every pair is connected by some path. 'Maximal' means you cannot add any more vertices to the component while keeping it connected. A graph with a single connected component is a connected graph; otherwise it is disconnected.

Finding all connected components is straightforward with BFS or DFS: run BFS/DFS from an unvisited vertex, mark everything reachable as component k, then find the next unvisited vertex and start component k+1. This outer loop runs once per component, and the inner BFS/DFS is O(V+E) total across all runs — so the overall algorithm is still **O(V + E)**.

Real-world applications of connected components: image processing (flood fill / blob detection — all pixels of the same colour that touch form a component); network analysis (which users can reach each other in a social network); dependency analysis (which packages in a repository are completely independent of each other); terrain generation (which land tiles belong to the same continent).

**For directed graphs**, connectivity is more subtle. Even if every vertex can be reached from vertex A, it does not mean you can return from any vertex back to A. **Strongly Connected Components (SCCs)** are the maximal subsets where every vertex can reach every other following directed edges. Tarjan's algorithm and Kosaraju's algorithm both find SCCs in O(V + E) using DFS. SCCs are used in compilers (finding mutually recursive functions), in deadlock detection (mutual waiting cycles), and in web analytics (finding tightly-knit communities in the link graph).

A useful mental model: **condense** the directed graph by collapsing each SCC into a single super-node. The resulting condensation graph is always a DAG — you can topologically sort the SCCs to get a high-level processing order.

sections.title: Weighted Graphs and Dijkstra's Algorithm
sections.content:
Everything so far assumed that all edges have the same cost — so 'shortest path' meant 'fewest edges'. In a **weighted graph** each edge carries a numeric weight, and the shortest path minimises the **total weight** (sum of edge weights along the path).

**Dijkstra's algorithm** solves single-source shortest paths on graphs with non-negative edge weights. It is a beautiful generalisation of BFS: instead of processing vertices in FIFO order (uniform cost), it processes them in order of current known distance from the source — using a **min-heap (priority queue)**.

The algorithm:
1. Set dist[source] = 0, dist[all others] = Infinity.
2. Push (0, source) into the min-heap.
3. Pop (d, u) — the vertex with the current minimum distance.
4. If d > dist[u], skip (this is a stale entry from an earlier update).
5. For each neighbour v of u with edge weight w: if dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v] and push (dist[v], v) into the heap.
6. Repeat until the heap is empty.

Time complexity: **O((V + E) log V)** with a binary heap, or O(E + V log V) with a Fibonacci heap. The log V factor comes from heap operations.

**Critical constraint: non-negative weights only.** Dijkstra fails with negative-weight edges because it assumes that once a vertex is popped from the heap its distance is final — but a negative edge encountered later could provide a shorter path. For graphs with negative weights, use **Bellman-Ford** (O(VE)) which relaxes all edges V−1 times. For all-pairs shortest paths, use **Floyd-Warshall** (O(V³)) which works with negative weights (but not negative cycles).

**When to choose which algorithm:**
- Unweighted graph, shortest hops → BFS, O(V+E)
- Weighted graph, non-negative weights, single source → Dijkstra, O((V+E) log V)
- Weighted graph, possibly negative weights, single source → Bellman-Ford, O(VE)
- All-pairs shortest paths → Floyd-Warshall, O(V³)
- Heuristic-guided shortest path (e.g., GPS routing) → A*, O((V+E) log V) with admissible heuristic

**Historical context worth knowing:** Graph theory was born in 1736 when Leonhard Euler solved the Königsberg Bridge Problem — could one walk across all seven bridges of Königsberg crossing each exactly once? Euler proved it was impossible by showing the city graph had more than two vertices of odd degree (which is required for an Eulerian path). This created the field of graph theory. Dijkstra's algorithm was conceived in 1956 by Edsger Dijkstra in about 20 minutes while sitting in a café in Amsterdam — he did not have paper and designed it to be executable in his head. He published it in 1959. BFS was formalised in the 1950s for peer-to-peer network communication, and DFS traces back to 19th-century maze-solving methods (Trémaux's algorithm, 1882).

**Interview pattern recognition — the most valuable graph skill:** The hardest part of a graph problem in an interview is not the algorithm — it is recognising that the problem IS a graph problem. Train yourself to look for these signals:
- 'Find the minimum number of X to transform Y into Z' → BFS on an implicit graph (classic: Word Ladder)
- 'Can you reach X from Y?' → BFS or DFS reachability
- 'Find all groups of connected X' → connected components with BFS/DFS
- 'Is there a circular dependency?' → directed cycle detection with DFS or Kahn's
- 'What order should tasks be performed?' → topological sort
- 'Shortest route with travel costs' → Dijkstra
- Grid problems (islands, rooms, mazes) → treat each cell as a vertex; adjacent cells share edges

A common mistake: using DFS when BFS is needed (or vice versa). Ask yourself: 'Do I need the shortest path, or just any path?' Shortest path (fewest edges) → BFS. Any path / structural info → DFS.

items: A **graph** G = (V, E) is a set of vertices and edges. It can be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted, cyclic or acyclic, connected or disconnected — and trees are a special case (connected acyclic graph with V−1 edges).

**Adjacency lists** use O(V+E) space and are the default for sparse graphs. **Adjacency matrices** use O(V²) space but give O(1) edge existence checks — only prefer them for dense graphs or constant-time edge queries.
**BFS** (queue, level-by-level) guarantees the **shortest path** in unweighted graphs and runs in O(V+E). Use it for minimum-hop distances, connected components, and bipartite checking.
**DFS** (stack or recursion, dive deep first) also runs in O(V+E) but does NOT guarantee shortest paths. Use it for cycle detection, topological sort, SCCs, and DFS entry/exit timestamps.
**Topological sort** orders DAG vertices so every directed edge u→v has u before v. Kahn's BFS-based algorithm also detects cycles: if the output contains fewer than V vertices, a cycle exists.
**Dijkstra's algorithm** finds single-source shortest paths in weighted graphs with non-negative weights in O((V+E) log V). For negative weights use Bellman-Ford; for all-pairs use Floyd-Warshall.

Pattern recognition is the key graph skill: grid problems, transformation puzzles, dependency orderings, and connectivity questions all map to standard graph algorithms once you identify them as such.

quiz.question: What is the space complexity of an adjacency list for a graph with V vertices and E edges?
options: O(V²)
O(V + E)
O(E²)
O(V × E)
quiz.explanation: An adjacency list stores one entry per vertex and one entry per directed edge — O(V) for the vertex array plus O(E) for all neighbour lists combined, totalling O(V+E). For undirected graphs each edge appears twice (once per endpoint), but that is still O(E) = O(2E).

quiz.question: Which graph traversal guarantees the shortest path (fewest edges) in an unweighted graph?
options: DFS — depth-first search
BFS — breadth-first search
Topological sort
Dijkstra's algorithm
quiz.explanation: BFS processes all vertices at distance k before any at distance k+1. The first time it reaches a vertex it has found the minimum-hop path. DFS might find a long winding path; topological sort does not find paths; Dijkstra handles weighted graphs.

quiz.question: In the three-colour DFS cycle detection algorithm, what does encountering a GRAY neighbour mean?
options: The neighbour has been fully processed and is safe
The neighbour has not been visited yet
The neighbour is currently on the DFS call stack — a back edge indicating a directed cycle
The neighbour belongs to a different connected component
quiz.explanation: GRAY marks a vertex that is currently being explored (on the DFS stack). An edge from u to a GRAY vertex v means v is an ancestor of u in the current DFS path — a back edge — which is precisely a directed cycle. Edges to BLACK (fully done) vertices are safe.

quiz.question: Kahn's topological sort finishes with only 4 of 6 vertices in the output. What does this tell you?
options: The graph is disconnected
The graph contains a directed cycle involving the missing 2 vertices
Some vertices have no outgoing edges
BFS was used instead of Kahn's algorithm
quiz.explanation: Kahn's algorithm enqueues vertices only when their in-degree reaches 0. Vertices trapped in a cycle never have all their incoming edges removed, so their in-degree never reaches 0 and they are never enqueued. Output length < V is the definitive cycle detection signal.

quiz.question: When is an adjacency matrix preferred over an adjacency list?
options: When the graph is sparse (few edges relative to vertices)
When memory is very limited
When the graph is dense and O(1) edge-existence checks are required
When the graph has weighted edges
quiz.explanation: Adjacency matrices offer O(1) edge-existence checks (matrix[u][v]), which is useful when algorithms need rapid 'does this edge exist?' queries on dense graphs. For sparse graphs, the O(V²) space overhead stores mostly zeros — wasteful and often prohibitive.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of both BFS and DFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
options: O(V²)
O(V log V)
O(V + E)
O(E log V)
quiz.explanation: Both BFS and DFS visit each vertex once and examine each edge once — O(V) + O(E) = O(V+E). For sparse graphs this is much better than O(V²). The adjacency list representation makes this achievable; a matrix representation would force O(V²) for neighbour iteration.

quiz.question: A problem asks for the 'minimum number of moves to solve a sliding puzzle'. Which algorithm and representation should you reach for?
options: DFS on an adjacency matrix
BFS on an implicit graph where each puzzle state is a vertex
Topological sort on a DAG of states
Dijkstra's algorithm on a weighted grid
quiz.explanation: 'Minimum number of moves' with uniform-cost moves means BFS. Model each reachable puzzle state as a vertex; add an edge between states reachable by one legal move. BFS finds the shortest path (fewest moves) from the initial state to the goal state. The graph is implicit — you generate neighbours on the fly.

quiz.question: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm fail on graphs with negative-weight edges?
options: Negative weights cause integer overflow in the priority queue
Dijkstra requires all weights to be distinct
Once a vertex is popped from the min-heap Dijkstra treats its distance as final, but a later negative edge could yield a shorter path
Dijkstra only works on directed graphs, not undirected
quiz.explanation: Dijkstra's correctness relies on the 'greedy choice' property: when a vertex is popped with distance d, no future path can be shorter because all remaining edge weights are non-negative. A negative edge can break this — a later, longer-hop path might have smaller total weight. Use Bellman-Ford for negative weights.

quiz.question: A graph with 7 vertices and 6 edges forms a single connected component with no cycles. What type of structure is this?
options: A complete graph
A directed acyclic graph (DAG)
A tree — a connected acyclic undirected graph with exactly V−1 edges
A bipartite graph
quiz.explanation: A connected undirected graph with no cycles and exactly V−1 edges is by definition a tree. Trees are the minimal connected graphs: remove any edge and the graph disconnects; add any edge and a cycle forms. This is why tree traversal algorithms (pre/in/post-order) are simply DFS applied to an acyclic graph.

quiz.question: What is a Strongly Connected Component (SCC) in a directed graph?
options: A subgraph where every vertex has the same in-degree and out-degree
A maximal set of vertices where every vertex can reach every other vertex following directed edges
A set of vertices with no outgoing edges to other components
Any subgraph with no directed cycles
quiz.explanation: An SCC is a maximal set of vertices S such that for every pair (u, v) in S, there exists a directed path from u to v AND from v to u. 'Maximal' means you cannot add any more vertices while keeping this mutual-reachability property. Tarjan's and Kosaraju's algorithms both find all SCCs in O(V+E).
